passage: Each September, the floating sea ice that covers the Arctic Ocean shrinks to its annual minimum extent before refreezing through the colder months. The National Snow and Ice Data Center has compiled monthly extent records since the late 1970s, and a research team analyzing those records by decade has argued that, although the average September extent has fallen across each successive decade, the single-year low points within each decade have fallen faster than the decadal averages have. The data shown in the table support this characterization because _______

questionTable.caption: September Arctic sea ice extent (million km²) by decade (NSIDC Sea Ice Index)

question: Which choice most effectively uses data from the table to support the claim?

choices.text: across the four decades shown, the mean September extent fell continuously, from 7.2 million km² in the 1980s to 4.6 million km² in the 2010s.
the lowest year recorded in the 1980s, 6.9 million km² in 1985, was higher than every subsequent decadal low and every subsequent decadal mean.
the 2010s mean extent of 4.6 million km² is the lowest of any decade in the table, exceeding the 2010s decadal low of 3.6 million km².
the lowest single year of the 2000s, 4.3 million km² in 2007, fell below the mean September extent of the 2010s, 4.6 million km², even though that decade had not yet begun.

explanation: The team's claim is specific: the single-year lows within each decade have fallen faster than the decadal means. To support it, a choice must compare the two columns in a way that shows the lows pulling ahead. Choice D does this directly: the 2000s low of 4.3 million km2 (2007) already falls below the 2010s mean of 4.6 million km2, so a decadal low has dropped beneath an average from a later decade, which is exactly what "falling faster" looks like. Choice A reports only the means falling and so speaks to one column alone. Choice C compares a mean and a low within the single 2010s decade, which says nothing about relative rates across decades. Choice B notes that the 1985 low tops every later figure, a true statement that supports a plain downward trend rather than the steeper decline of the lows.
